config.text:
Workflow 1 — Targeted Reservoir Analysis


Goal: Quickly find everything ReSST knows about a specific dam, reservoir, or monitored reach—then review linked literature and export results. Use this workflow when: You already have a site in mind (by name, location, or known dam). What you’ll get: A site summary (key attributes) + the Site-linked Literature tied to that site, plus relevant General Literature you can compare against. Tip: Start broad (select the site), then narrow with filters only if needed.


Step 1: Find the site (Search or map navigation)

Use the Search box to type a reservoir/dam/site name (or a place name), OR Pan/zoom the Map to your area of interest. What to look for: The site point(s) on the map (dams/reservoirs/reaches). Result: You’re viewing the correct area and can select the site.


Step 2: Select the site on the map

Click the site point on the Map. If multiple features are close together, select the correct one from the selection list (if prompted). Result: The site becomes the active selection, and the app updates the right panel and tables.


Step 3: Review the Selected Data panel (site context)

In Selected Data (right panel), review the site’s key attributes (examples: Site Type, Sediment Release, Ecological Concern, Analysis). Why it matters: These attributes help you quickly determine whether this site is a useful analog for your project. Result: You understand the site’s basic context and “why it’s in the database.”


Step 4: Open the Site Literature tab (linked references)

In the Data Table, open the Site Literature tab. Scan titles/metadata and open links as needed. Tip: Site Literature is the fastest way to see what’s been documented for that location. Result: You’ve identified the references directly associated with the selected site.


Step 5: Compare with General Literature (broader methods + context)

Switch to the General Literature tab. Look for methods, monitoring approaches, modeling types, or ecological considerations relevant to your site. Tip: General literature is not tied to one site—use it to broaden your reading list. Result: You’ve expanded from “site-specific” to “methods and themes.”


Step 6: (Optional) Refine using Keyword Filters

Open Keyword Filters (left panel). Toggle one or more filters (examples: Sediment Characteristic, Sediment Release mechanism, Ecological Concern, Modeling Methods). Best practice: Add filters one at a time so you can see what changes. Result: The map and tables update to only show matching records.


Step 7: Export your results for offline review

In the Data Table, export the currently filtered/selected records (Sites and/or Literature tabs). Save as Excel/CSV (or use in GIS) for comparison, tracking, or reporting. Result: You have a portable dataset and reading list for your project files.

config.text: The Reservoir Sustainable Sediment Tool (ReSST) is a web-based application developed to compile and synthesize case studies, analytical approaches, and literature related to sediment release from reservoirs. ReSST is intended to support reservoir managers and environmental engineers by providing a centralized, searchable resource to explore precedent projects, sediment management strategies, ecological concerns, and analytical methods across sites and regions. ReSST allows users to interact with an interactive map, apply keyword-based filters, review sites and general literature, and export results for analysis. Workflow examples are available in the Help button on the toolbar.

config.text:
Workflow 2 — Regional Analysis by Hydrologic Unit Code (HUC)


Goal: Summarize sites and literature within a basin/sub-basin by selecting an area that matches a HUC boundary (HUC-2 / 4 / 6 / 8). Use this workflow when: You’re scoping sediment management needs or knowledge gaps for a watershed or district area. What you’ll get: A basin-focused set of Sites + associated Site Literature, plus relevant General Literature.


Step 1: Turn on the HUC layer you need

Open the Layer List / Reference Layers control. Turn on the desired HUC layer (HUC-2, HUC-4, HUC-6, or HUC-8). Tip: Start with a larger HUC (e.g., HUC-4) for screening, then move to smaller units for detail. Result: HUC boundaries appear on the map.


Step 2: Navigate to your basin (Bookmarks or pan/zoom)

Use Bookmarks (if available) to jump to a region, OR Pan/zoom the map to your basin of interest. Result: The basin boundary is visible and ready for selection.


Step 3: Use Spatial Selection to capture sites in the HUC

Activate the Spatial Selection tool (near the search/tools area). Draw a polygon by roughly tracing the HUC boundary (you don’t need to be perfect). What happens next: Any sites intersecting your polygon are selected automatically. Result: The Selected Data and tables update to your region.


Step 4: Confirm the selection in the Sites tab

In the Data Table, open the Sites tab. Confirm the number and distribution of selected sites matches your intent. Tip: If you got too many or too few, redraw the polygon or adjust the map scale. Result: You have a clean basin-based site set.


Step 5: Review Site Literature for the basin

Switch to Site Literature. Scan for repeated themes (e.g., dredging vs drawdown, fish passage, water quality, modeling approaches). Result: You’ve identified what’s been studied in the basin—and what hasn’t.


Step 6: (Optional) Use filters to focus within the region

Open Keyword Filters and refine within the selected HUC (examples: Sediment Source = bank erosion; Ecological Concern = water quality; Analysis = sediment transport modeling). Result: You’re narrowing the basin results to your technical question.


Step 7: Export basin results (sites + literature)

Export Sites, Site Literature, and/or General Literature based on your current selection and filters. Result: You have a basin summary dataset for offline analysis, reporting, or comparison across HUCs.

Workflow 3 — River Length Compilation (Corridor/Multiple Dams)


Goal: Build a corridor-scale dataset by selecting all Sites along a named river or multi-dam reach, then compiling linked literature. Use this workflow when: You’re evaluating sediment continuity, a multi-dam system, or downstream effects along a river corridor. What you’ll get: A longitudinal “corridor” set of Sites + literature you can review and export as one package.


Step 1: Define your corridor (river name + extent)

Decide your corridor start/end (e.g., “Dam A to Dam D” or “Headwaters to confluence”). Navigate to the corridor using Search (river/place) and/or Bookmarks. Result: You’re viewing the corridor at a scale where multiple sites are visible.


Step 2: Select sites along the corridor

Option A: Use Spatial Selection to draw a long, narrow polygon following the river, OR

Option B: Use Select-by-layer (if available) and repeat selections in segments. Tip: Work in segments if the corridor is long—then export each segment or merge later offline. Result: Sites along the river corridor are selected.


Step 3: Validate the corridor selection (Sites tab)

Open the Sites tab in the data table. Sort or scan the list to confirm you captured the sites you intended (and didn’t include unrelated nearby sites). Result: Your corridor selection is accurate.


Step 4: Compile linked literature for the corridor

Open the Site Literature tab. Review the references linked to the selected corridor sites. Tip: Look for patterns by method (monitoring vs modeling), release type (drawdown, dredging, etc.), and ecological concerns (fish passage, water quality). Result: You’ve assembled corridor-specific literature.


Step 5: Add General Literature to round out methods

Switch to General Literature. Use it to find broader guidance, modeling approaches, or monitoring methods relevant to your corridor.

Result: A more complete corridor reading list.


Step 6: (Optional) Focus the corridor dataset with filters

Use Keyword Filters to focus (examples: Sediment Characteristic = gravel; Analysis = 2D/3D modeling; Special Cases = wildfire/landslides if relevant).

Result: Corridor results targeted to your study objective.


Step 7: Export for longitudinal review

Export the corridor’s Sites and Literature tables. Use the export for a longitudinal comparison (upstream → downstream) in Excel or GIS. Result: A corridor-scale dataset ready for analysis and documentation.

config.text:
Workflow 4 — Thematic or Categorical Review


Goal: Find literature and sites that match a technical theme, regardless of region—using ReSST’s controlled keyword filters. Use this workflow when: You’re building a reading list, comparing methods, or looking for analogs across different watersheds. What you’ll get: A cross-basin set of Sites and Literature filtered by theme (e.g., sediment type, ecological concern, modeling method, release mechanism).


Step 1: Choose a theme (what are you trying to compare?)

Examples of good themes:

Sediment Characteristic: cohesive / sand / gravel / suspended / bedload

Sediment Release mechanism: drawdown / dredging / dam removal / normal operations

Ecological Concern: fish passage / water quality / endangered species Analysis /

Modeling Methods: field monitoring / 1D-2D-3D modeling / sediment transport modeling.

Result: You have a clear filter strategy before you click anything.


Step 2: Open Keyword Filters and select your first filter

Expand Keyword Filters (left panel). Pick a category and toggle one value (start with one!). Tip: Starting with one filter helps you avoid “zero results” frustration. Result: The map and tables immediately update to the theme.


Step 3: Add a second filter to narrow (optional but common)

Add a second category to sharpen the theme (example: Sediment Characteristic = gravel + Channel Type = braided rivers).

Result: You’re now looking at a targeted subset across basins.


Step 4: Review results in the map and tables

Scan the Map to see where matching sites occur. Use the Site Literature and General Literature tabs to build your reading list. Result: You can quickly identify clusters, gaps, and transferable methods.


Step 5: Use Selected Data to spot strong analogs

Click a promising site on the map. Review the Selected Data panel to confirm its key attributes match your needs. Tip: This is the fastest “is this relevant?” check. Result: You’ve identified best-fit analog sites and references.


Step 6: Export the filtered theme results

Export Site Literature and/or General Literature as your theme-based reading list. (Optional) Export the Sites table to map/compare candidates offline. Result: A shareable reading list and comparison dataset.


Step 7: Clear filters to start a new theme

Clear or reset filters before starting a new theme. Result: You avoid “stacked filters” that accidentally hide results.

Welcome to RESST


The Reservoir Sustainable Sediment Tool (ReSST) is a web-based application developed to compile and synthesize case studies, analytical approaches, and literature related to sediment release from reservoirs. ReSST is intended to support reservoir managers and environmental engineers by providing a centralized, searchable resource to explore precedent projects, sediment management strategies, ecological concerns, and analytical methods across sites and regions. The beta version of ReSST allows users to interact with an interactive map, apply keyword-based filters, review sites and general literature, and export results for analysis.


On the below tabs are examples of different workflows that RESST can be used for.
